list.listitem: Obtain a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS) in the initial evaluation of a thyroid nodule. B

Ultrasound for thyroid nodule evaluation identifies nodules at risk of being malignant. The ACR TI-RADS system can be used to risk stratify based on ultrasound appearance and size, with fine needle aspiration biopsy only of larger, high risk lesions (>= 2.5 cm if mildly suspicious, >= 1.5 cm if moderately suspicious, and >= 1 cm if highly suspicious based on TI-RADS ultrasound classification). C
Current symptoms, past medical history, family history, and physical examination findings identify patients with increased risk for thyroid nodule malignancy. C
Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (US-FNA) should be based on the TI-RADS thyroid nodule evaluation criteria for malignancy. B

If TSH level is low and free thyroxine is elevated, thyroid scintigraphy should be performed; thyroid nodules determined to be hyperactive (hot) do not require FNA; nodules that are hypoactive (cold) or normoactive should be managed based on TI-RADS criteria.B

background.definition: A thyroid nodule is a discrete lesion within the parenchyma of the thyroid gland. Most thyroid nodules are asymptomatic, and 95% are benign. Symptoms can include dysphagia, dyspnea, cough, cervical or neck pain, hoarseness, choking sensation, or symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

list.listitem: The estimated annual incidence rate in the US of thyroid nodules identified by palpation is 0.1% or about 300,000 nodules. This number does not include the majority of nodules which are identified incidentally during imaging studies for other reasons.
The Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Cancer Program reported 13.71 cases per 100,000 persons per year with approximately 45,000 new thyroid cancer cases in 2019.

The prevalence of a thyroid nodule found by palpation is 4% to 7% of the population but actual prevalence may be as high as 68% when nodules found incidentally through imaging for other reasons (the incidentalomas) are included.
Nodules are more common in women and in the elderly.
Twenty percent to forty eight percent of patients with a palpable thyroid nodule are found to have additional nodules on ultrasound (US).
Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine cancer.

Malignant thyroid nodules can be induced by exposure to head and neck irradiation as a child and by exposure to atomic blasts or nuclear accidents. Childhood irradiation was used to treat acne, enlarged thymus glands, enlarged tonsils or adenoids, and Hodgkin's disease.
Malignant thyroid nodules can be hereditary, like familial medullary carcinoma (MTC) and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2).
Benign thyroid nodules and goiter formation can be promoted by iodine deficiency.
Benign thyroid nodules can be caused by preexisting thyroid diseases such as multinodular goiter (MNG), Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and subacute thyroiditis.

In a case series of 120 Italian pediatric patients with thyroid nodules, 6 had hyperthyroidism (1 Hurthle cell and 5 follicular adenomas) and the remainder were euthyroid (33 hyperplasic nodules, 19 carcinomas [14 papillary, 3 follicular, and 2 medullary], 3 follicular and 1 Hurthle cell adenoma, and 1 teratoma).

The thyroid is composed of two main cell types, follicular cells and parafollicular cells, or C cells. The two well-differentiated carcinomas, papillary and follicular, develop in the follicle cells. Medullary cancer originates in the C cells.

Papillary adenocarcinoma is the most common malignant thyroid nodule, occurring in 75% to 80%. It occurs 2 to 3 times more frequently in women and accounts for 85% of thyroid malignancies that are due to radiation exposure. Cervical lymphadenopathy is common, and blood-borne metastatic spread is rare. Hurtle cell carcinoma, a variant of papillary carcinoma, is more aggressive.

Follicular carcinoma accounts for 10% to 20% of the malignant thyroid nodules and is more aggressive. Metastatic spread is by blood vessel invasion and not lymphatic spread. Incidence increases with age and is more common in women. It is rarely associated with irradiation exposure.

Medullary carcinoma, sporadic and familial, accounts for 3% to 5% of the malignant thyroid nodules. The tumor can secrete markers such as calcitonin, prostaglandins, and serotonin. Assessment for MTC and MEN2 includes calcitonin levels and a genetic study for the oncogene, rearranged in transformation/papillary thyroid carcinoma (ret/PTC). Regional metastatic spread to the neck lymph nodes occurs early, and spread to distant organs such as lung, liver, bone, brain, and adrenal occurs late.

Anaplastic carcinoma, accounting for 1% to 2% of thyroid cancers, is responsible for approximately 50% of all thyroid cancer deaths. It spreads rapidly to lymph nodes, trachea, and other organs, especially lungs and bone. 6-month overall survival is 35% and there is nearly 100% disease-specific mortality.
Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, sarcomas, and metastatic disease to the thyroid are rare.
The most common benign thyroid nodules are follicular adenomas and cysts.
It is not clear if single nodules in patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis are more likely to be malignant.

Differential.Differential_Features: Tender thyroid, elevated sedimentation rate, thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TpAb)
Increased parathyroid hormone and calcium, myalgias, nausea
Ultrasound for anatomic location and composition
Skin opening in neck (midline), tenderness, and erythema if infected
Men in their 20s-30s, elevated beta-human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein, cough
X-ray of the lateral soft tissues of the neck

list.listitem: Patients may present for evaluation of a thyroid nodule that was found by observation or palpation by the patient. The physician may discover the nodule during a neck exam. Thyroid nodules can be found incidentally on studies such as a carotid US or a cervical MRI. The absence of symptoms does not exclude malignancy.
Suspicious history for a thyroid carcinoma includes head and neck irradiation as a child or exposure to a nuclear accident, and persistent dyspnea, dysphagia, or hoarseness/voice changes.
Also ask about any change in the mass, dyspnea, dysphagia, or dysphonia, and use of iodine containing drugs or supplements. A positive family history also raises suspicion for MTC or MEN2.
Suspicious physical examination findings for a thyroid carcinoma are a firm nodule, rapid growth of the lesion, fixation to adjacent structures, cervical lymphadenopathy, and vocal cord paralysis.
Children and adolescents with a thyroid nodule are more likely to have malignancy but also have a better prognosis.
The initial step in evaluating a palpated thyroid nodule or one identified on other imaging modality is to obtain TSH level and high resolution thyroid ultrasound.

If the TSH is low, thyroid scintigraphy should be performed to assess whether the nodule is “hot” or “cold”.
Hyperfunctioning (hot) nodules do not require FNA; treatment for hyperthyroidism should be addressed. Hypofunctioning (cold) nodules or normal functioning nodules should then be addressed based on ultrasound findings as below. As with other nodules in the thyroid, most “cold” nodules are benign.
If the TSH is normal or elevated, the nodule is evaluated by ultrasound using the TI-RADS criteria (below); a patient with an elevated TSH should also be assessed and treated for hypothyroidism.

There is a positive correlation between the TSH level and the likelihood of a nodule being malignant. Low TSH levels favor a benign nodule and higher TSH levels (even within the “normal” range) increase the likelihood of malignancy.

High resolution thyroid ultrasound should be performed to evaluate all nodules. The combination of size of the nodule and certain features found on ultrasound determine whether FNA is needed. US features associated with thyroid carcinoma are microcalcifications, hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, solid, intranodule vascularity determined by Doppler, and shape taller than wider. No one US feature can independently predict malignant lesions. The presence of two features increases the diagnostic accuracy from 87% to 93%. Interrater reliability is moderate (kappa = 0.49 for 3D ultrasound images, only 0.15 for 2D images).

In 2017, the TI-RADS (Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System) classification system was proposed by the American College of Radiology. It assigns points to lesions based on their composition, echogenecity, shape, margin, and presence of echogenic foci. An online calculator is found here. The guideline recommends follow-up intervals of no less than 1 year, with interval and duration based on risk (below).
0 points (TR-1): Benign, no fine needle aspiration (FNA) needed 1 to 2 points (TR-2): Not suspicious, no FNA needed. 3 points (TR-3): Mildly suspicious, FNA if >= 2.5 cm, follow if >= 1.5 cm but <2.5 cm. Follow-up scans at 1, 3 and 5 years. 4 to 6 points (TR-4): Moderately suspicious, FNA if >= 1.5 cm, follow if >= 1 cm but <1.5 cm. Follow-up scans at 1, 2, 3 and 5 years 7 or more points (TR-5): Highly suspicious, FNA if >= 1 cm, follow if >= 5 mm but <1 cm. Follow-up scans annually for 5 years.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies with 18,614 patients showed that the TI-RADS system offers favourable risk stratification with sensitivity of 0.89 and specificity of 0.70. A systematic review comparing the ACR TI-RADS with AI TI-RADS and with British Thyroid Cancer Guidelines demonstrated similar high sensitivity across the 3 systems. Another recent systematic review compared five different ultrasound risk stratification systems, and found ACR TI-RADS to have higher specificity and diagnostic odds ratio, but lower sensitivity, resulting in fewer FNA proceduress; the decreased sensitivity is mitigated by scheduled follow up ultrasounds.

Artificial intelligence is being studied as a way to augment physician interpretation of ultrasounds. While promising, one study found that it had similar sensitivity but lower specificity than ACR TI-RADS.

There is no clear linear association between nodule size and the risk of malignancy. In a series of over 7000 nodules, the overall rate of malignancy was 13%. The rate was 10% between 1 and 1.9 cm, and 15% greater than 2.0 cm, but there was no difference between 2.0 to 2.9, 3.0 to 3.9 and >4 cm nodules.
Ultrasound is also recommended for patients at risk for thyroid malignancy, patients with multinodular goiter and patients with lymphadenopathy suggestive of a malignant lesion.
Contrast enhanced US has been shown in a meta-analysis of 33 studies to have high sensitivity and specificity (both 88%, LR+ 7.2, LR- 0.13) in differentiating malignant from benign thyroid nodules.

US elastography is an option for patients with indeterminate nodules on FNA. In one study of 51 consecutive patients referred for surgical treatment of single, solid thyroid nodules less than 10 mm, a real-time score of 4 to 5 diagnosed papillary thyroid microcarcinomas with a sensitivity of 91% and specificity or 89%.
In a study of 36 patients with solid thyroid nodules, MRI was 86% sensitive and 100% specific for identification of papillary carcinomas.

Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNA) is recommended to diagnose thyroid malignancy. Selection of nodules should be by the US features for malignancy and size (). US-FNA increases accuracy and diagnostic yield; the inadequate specimen rate decreased from 11% to 7% in one study, and cytologic accuracy of malignancy increased from 61% to 80%. FNA biopsy results can be divided into 5 categories: nondiagnostic (10%-20%, should be <15% in good hands), malignant (5%-15%), follicular lesion (20%), suspicious (5%), or benign (60%-75%). There was no difference in accuracy of FNA biopsy by nodule size (<4 cm vs ≥4 cm).

A meta-analysis identified 36 studies with 16, 597 patients evaluating the accuracy of fine needle biopsy for the diagnosis of thyroid malignancy. It was 86% sensitive, 71% specific, LR+ was 3.0 and LR- was 0.2.

The use of scintigraphy is limited in the workup of thyroid nodules. Radionuclide thyroid scans determine the functionality of the nodules by the pattern of uptake, and they differentiate hypofunctioning (cold) from hyperfunctioning (hot) nodules. The majority, 77% to 94%, of thyroid nodules identified by scintigraphy are cold, and should have an FNA if TI-RADS criteria are met. The risk of malignancy of a cold nodule is 5% to 8%. Autonomously functioning thyroid nodules in adults need no further cytologic evaluation because the incidence of malignancy is exceedingly low. Technetium or radioiodide are used for scintigraphy.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography infrequently identifies nodules, but nodules when found have a high risk of malignancy and should undergo HRUS followed by FNA biopsy.

In a small study (n = 42 nodules, 28 benign and 14 papillary carcinomas), MRI was 86% sensitive and 100% specific for diagnosing cancer. Similar findings were seen in a study of 25 patients with scintigraphyically cold nodules.
Research is ongoing to improve the diagnostic accuracy for malignancy in thyroid nodules, such as cancer gene expression profiling studies.
Thyroglobulin antibodies may act as marker for papillary thyroid cancer in patients with indeterminate nodules.
An algorithm is seen in .
A nonpalpable nodule has the same risk of malignancy as a palpable nodule of the same size.
Palpable and nonpalpable nodules have the same risk of malignancy as nodules found in a multinodular goiter.

TI-RADS recommended follow up US for nodules that do not meet FNA criteria are listed above. Following are recommendations from the American Thyroid Association (ATA) for nodules that do not meet their FNA criteria:
Nodules with high suspicion ultrasound pattern: follow up US in 6 to 12 months Nodules with low to intermediate suspicion pattern: follow up US in 12 to 24 months Nodules > 1cm in size with very low suspicion pattern: may consider repeat US in 24 months Nodules 1 cm or less in size with very low suspicion pattern do not require US follow up

Per ATA, these are “weak” recommendations based on low-quality evidence (exception is nodules > 1cm with very low suspicion pattern; ATA says this is “no recommendation” and based on insufficient evidence)
Asymptomatic patients with cytologically benign nodules have a very low risk of subsequently developing malignancy.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening for thyroid cancer in asymptomatic adults by palpation or by ultrasound. This recommendation is for average-risk individuals and does not include those at higher risk for thyroid malignancy.

Ultrasound screening may be considered in individuals at higher risk for thyroid malignancy (i.e. significant exposure to radiation, family history of thyroid cancer); this is likely to catch cancers at earlier stage, however effects on mortality have not been shown.

An observational study identified 992 consecutive patients with asymptomatic, benign thyroid nodules. Over 5 years, 11% grew at least 20% in size, on average from 11 to 18 mm in diameter. Growth was more likely in patients with more nodules, with larger nodules, in patients under age 45 years, and in men. Nodules shrank in a similar number of patients. Cancer was subsequently diagnosed in 5 nodules (0.3%), of which only 2 had grown over the follow-up period.

A retrospective cohort study identified 393 patients with a single thyroid nodule and non-diagnostic FNA results who had adequate follow-up. Ultimately, 2.3% were diagnosed with cancer. Patients with cancer were older than those without (mean age 63 years vs 55 years), were more likely to be men (OR 4.2), and in those with initially larger nodules.

For patients with papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, recurrence following surgery was shown to be rare on a large retrospective cohort study (n=1636). This supports de-escalation of follow-up in this patient group.
For the most part, thyroid cancer has a favorable prognosis. The five-year relative survival rate (excludes other causes of death) for individuals with thyroid cancer is 98.3%.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the Diagnosis of Thyroid Nodule.

cell.label: Thyroid nodule found on palpation or by imaging.
Check TSH and obtain high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS).
FNA not needed. Consider treatment for hyperthyroidism.
Apply TI-RADS criteria, based on ultrasound, to determine whether FNA is indicated.*
cell.path: Does not meet TI-RADS criteria for FNA

cell.label: Follow-up ultrasound based on the TI-RADS level.**

footnotes.footnote: *FNA by TI-RADS level and size: TR3 (mildly suspicious) 2.5 cm or larger; TR4 (moderately suspicious) 1.5 cm or larger; TR5 (highly suspicious) 1 cm or larger. TR1 and TR2 nodules need no FNA.
**Follow-up ultrasound: TR3 nodules 1.5 to 2.4 cm at 1, 3, and 5 years; TR4 nodules 1 to 1.4 cm at 1, 2, 3, and 5 years; TR5 nodules 0.5 to 0.9 cm every year for 5 years.
TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone; HRUS, high-resolution ultrasound; FNA, fine needle aspiration; TI-RADS, American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System.
